entries.title: Gujarati at a glance
body: Gujarati is the Indo-Aryan language of Gujarat in western India, with about 55 million speakers and large communities in East Africa, Britain and North America. Mahatma Gandhi's first language was Gujarati.
The verb comes last, nouns are masculine, feminine or neuter, and postpositions are joined to the end of the noun.

entries.title: How the script works
body: The Gujarati script grew out of Devanagari and is easy to compare with it: most letters have the same structure, but Gujarati drops the line along the top. Each consonant carries a short a, other vowels are marks around it, and full vowel letters start a word.
Unlike Hindi, Gujarati uses the ordinary full stop and comma rather than the danda।

entries.title: “To be” and the present
entries.body: The present tense is the stem with a person ending, followed by the matching form of છે. The negative uses -તો / -તી / -તું and નથી.

entries.title: Three genders
entries.body: Gujarati keeps the neuter gender that Hindi lost. Adjectives and possessives ending in a vowel follow the noun.

entries.title: Postpositions
entries.body: These are written joined to the noun. A masculine noun in -ો becomes -ા before them.

entries.title: Navratri and garba
entries.body: Navratri, the nine nights in honour of the goddess Durga in autumn, is Gujarat's biggest festival. Every evening people dance garba and dandiya raas in circles, often until dawn. Gujarati food is largely vegetarian and is served as a thali with a little of many dishes.
